raw_response:
Alright, let me think through this year's plan for my stevia.

I've been doing stevia for a few years now. It's not like wheat or maize where everyone in the village knows what to do — stevia is more of a specialty thing, and the buyer (the contracting company) gives us some guidance. My 3 mu is small, so I put all of it in stevia because the price per mu is better than grain. If I planted wheat-maize I'd barely clear anything after inputs.

The company provides seedlings — they come around late April. I transplant right after. Last year I got my seedlings a bit late and it cost me, so this year I'm ready to go as soon as they deliver. I prepare the field in early April, plow once with a rented tractor (the neighbor with the machine charges me about 40 yuan per mu), then I rake it smooth by hand with my wife. We lay drip tape or furrows — I use furrow because drip tape I can't afford to replace every year.

For fertilizer, stevia likes it but you can't overdo nitrogen or the leaves get bitter and the company pays less. Last year I used about 15 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) per mu as base before transplanting, then topdressed urea twice — about 8 kg per mu each time, once after the plants took root and once after the first cut. That worked okay. I'll do the same this year. The extension guy mentioned potassium helps the leaf quality but potash is expensive and I just use the compound.

Irrigation — this is where stevia is different from wheat. It can't dry out, especially after transplanting and after each cut. I pump from the well 4-5 times during the season, maybe more if June is hot. The electricity for pumping adds up, maybe 80-100 yuan per mu for the year.

Pests — stevia gets some leaf miners and occasionally aphids. I spray insecticide maybe twice, and I spot-spray herbicide between the rows early on. Mostly I weed by hand because the plants are small and I don't want to damage them. That's a lot of work — my wife and I do most of it, and my mother helps when she can.

Harvest is the big labor push. We cut twice — first cut around late July, second cut early September. The company sends people to buy the dried leaves, so we cut, spread them out to dry on tarps in the yard for 3-4 days, bag them up. My two kids are in school so they only help on weekends. For the main harvest I might hire one or two neighbors for a couple days — 120 yuan a day plus lunch.

Yield-wise, last year I got about 280 kg of dry leaves per mu across both cuts. If the weather cooperates I'm hoping for 300 this year but I won't count on it. Price was around 12 yuan per kg last year from the contract — I hope it holds.
